key_insight: High MRI tumor classification scores can be misleading because public benchmark splits contain multiple kinds of data leakage that inflate performance.
clinical_relevance: For medical imaging research, a strong leaderboard result does not prove a model truly learned tumor biology unless training and test data are independent at the image, patient, and source levels.
method: Audited three widely used brain-tumor MRI corpora for duplicate, patient, and source-label contamination.
Compared effects across nine model architectures and three evaluation conditions.
Used a chest-radiograph negative control to test whether non-anatomical file-header cues could still separate classes.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports severe contamination, including 28.8% near-duplicate leakage in one test split, 22.3% byte-identical leakage in another, 95.5% patient-level sharing in traceable cases, and balanced accuracy of 0.959 from file-header features alone.
watch_item: Removing identified leaked images did not materially change balanced accuracy, so deduplication alone may not be enough to certify benchmark integrity.
paper_title: Scores That Hold, Benchmarks That Leak: Measuring Dataset Contamination in Public Brain-Tumor MRI Classification
